title: The Derivative - Introduction
Interpreting the Derivative
text:
When \(f(t)\) measures the position of an object in motion at time \(t\), the instantaneous rate of change \(f'(a)\) has a familiar meaning: it is the object’s instantaneous velocity at the moment \(t=a\). But derivatives show up in many contexts that have nothing to do with motion. What does the instantaneous rate of change mean in general when \(f(x)\) models the relationship between two variables \(x\) and \(y\)?
In general, the derivative of \(y=f(x)\) measures how sensitive the output \(y\) is to small, local changes in the input \(x\). If \(f'(a)\) is large in magnitude, then even a small change in \(x\) near \(x=a\) produces a large change in \(y\). If \(f'(a)\) is close to \(0\), then small changes in \(x\) near \(x=a\) barely affect \(y\) at all.


This gives us a practical way to interpret \(f'(a)\) in any context. We use it to estimate how much \(y\) changes when \(x\) changes by a small amount. Since \(f'(a)\) is the limit of average rates of change \(\frac{\Delta y}{\Delta x}\) over smaller and smaller intervals around \(x=a\), for a small change \(\Delta x\) we expect \[\frac{\Delta y}{\Delta x}\approx f'(a).\] Multiplying both sides by \(\Delta x\) gives us the key relationship for this section.






NotePractical Interpretation of \(f'(a)\)



If \(x\) changes from \(x=a\) to \(x=a+\Delta x\), where \(\Delta x\) is small, then the corresponding change in \(y=f(x)\) is approximately \[\Delta y \approx f'(a)\,\Delta x.\] In particular, the units of \(f'(a)\) are the units of \(y\) per unit of \(x\).


Keep in mind that this is a local estimate: it is only reliable when \(\Delta x\) is small, because the rate of change of \(f(x)\) may be quite different at points far away from \(x=a\).
How small does \(\Delta x\) need to be? As we will see, that depends on the context and how sensitive we expect the rate of change to be to changes in \(x\).

title: Definition of the Derivative
text:
Today, we will generalize our idea of instantaneous velocity. Given any function \(f(x)\), we can try to measure its instantaneous rate of change at a given point \(x=a\) by computing its average rate of change over smaller and smaller intervals around \(x=a\).
As the width of these intervals shrinks down to \(0\), if the values of the average rate of change appear to be approaching some real number \(m\), we will take this value to be our instantaneous rate of change. We call this value the derivative of \(f(x)\) at \(x=a\) and will use the notation \(f'(a)\) to represent it symbolically.
As we saw with instantaneous velocity, we can write this definition of \(f'(a)\) precisely in terms of limits.

Definition 1 (Derivative at a Point) The derivative of \(f(x)\) at \(x=a\), or \(f'(a)\), is
\[f'(a)=\lim_{x\to a}\frac{f(x)-f(a)}{x-a}\]

Instead of writing this limit in terms of a point \(x\) that is getting closer and closer to \(a\) (from both sides), we could also write it in terms of the width (and direction) of the interval on which we are computing the average rate of change. This is equivalent to a change of variables in the previous formula. Letting \(h=x-a\), we get:

Definition 2 (Derivative at a Point - Interval Version) \[ f'(a)=\lim_{h\to 0}\frac{f(a+h)-f(a)}{h}\]

title: Limits & Continuity - Introduction
text: Creating the proper tools that allow us to measure rate and accumulation require us to grapple with infinities and infinitesimals. Here are some examples that illustrate the logical hurdle these ideas pose:

title: Limits & Continuity - Introduction
Limits & Continuity - Introduction
text:
Big Idea
Paradoxes or controversies are not allowed in mathematics. They are the result of a lack of clarity. Either the question has not been posed clearly, terms have not been clearly defined, or assumptions have not been clearly stated.
The key idea that we will need before we can proceed to our main goals is the limit. In this unit, we will define limits, develop our conceptual understanding of them, and determine some rules and algebraic procedures that can be used to compute some types of limits precisely.

title: Limit Properties
text:
Now that we have some intuition about what a limit of a function is and what it means for a function to be continuous, we can dig a little deeper into how these ideas work and how they can be applied.
First, let’s consider what happens when we take the limit of a combination of functions. If we know that \(\lim_{x\to a}f(x)=L\) and \(\lim_{x\to a}g(x)=M\), can we figure out what happens when we compute the limit of some combination of \(f(x)\) and \(g(x)\)? For example, your intuition probably tells you that \(S(x)=f(x)+g(x)\) will approach \(L+M\) as \(x\) approaches \(a\), but can we explain why this is correct?
Take an \(x\)-value close to \(a\), say \(x=a+t\) where \(t\) is a small positive or negative number. Since \(\lim_{x\to a}f(x)=L\) and \(\lim_{x\to a}g(x)=M\), we know that \(f(a+t)=L+\epsilon\) and \(g(a+t)=M+\delta\), where \(\epsilon\) and \(\delta\) are themselves small — the closer \(x\) is to \(a\) (the smaller \(t\) is), the smaller \(\epsilon\) and \(\delta\) get.
Adding these together, \[\begin{align}
S(a+t)& =f(a+t)+g(a+t)\\
& =(L+\epsilon)+(M+\delta) \\
& =L+M+(\epsilon+\delta).
\end{align}\] Since \(\epsilon\) and \(\delta\) are both small, their sum \(\epsilon+\delta\) is small too.
Now let \(x\) get closer and closer to \(a\): \(t\) shrinks toward \(0\), which forces \(\epsilon\) and \(\delta\) — and therefore \(\epsilon+\delta\) — to shrink toward \(0\) as well. That’s exactly what it means for \(S(x)=f(x)+g(x)\) to approach \(L+M\) as \(x\to a\).
Similar reasoning can help you figure out and explain the properties listed in the following theorem. These properties are listed in terms of two-sided limits, but they also apply to one-sided limits, and limits as \(x\to \pm\infty\):







Theorem 1 (Limit Properties) If \[\lim_{x\to a}f(x)=L \text{ and } \lim_{x\to a}g(x)=M,\] then:

\(\displaystyle\lim_{x\to a}\left[f(x)\pm g(x)\right]=L\pm M\)
\(\displaystyle\lim_{x\to a}\left[f(x)\cdot g(x)\right]=L\cdot M\)
\(\displaystyle\lim_{x\to a}\left[\frac{f(x)}{g(x)}\right]=\frac{L}{M},~~\) as long as \(M\neq 0\)

title: The Second Derivative
text:
We already have a good understanding of functions with constant slope. These are linear functions, and their graphs are straight lines. If the slope is positive, the function is increasing; if the slope is negative, the function is decreasing.
Over the past few sections, we developed a way to measure the slope of a function when the slope is not constant: the derivative \(f'(x)\) tells us the slope of \(f(x)\) at each point. When the slope of a function is always changing, its graph is no longer a straight line. Instead, the graph bends and curves.
In this section, we will measure how the slope itself is changing. Since \(f'(x)\) is a function, we can take its derivative to find the rate of change of the slope of \(f(x)\).

Definition 1 (The Second Derivative) The second derivative of \(f(x)\), written \(f''(x)\), is the derivative of \(f'(x)\): \[f''(x)=\lim_{h\to 0}\frac{f'(x+h)-f'(x)}{h}.\] The value \(f''(a)\) measures the instantaneous rate of change of the slope of \(f(x)\) at \(x=a\).

Our goal is to use \(f''(x)\) to understand how the graph of \(f(x)\) is curved, in the same way that we use \(f'(x)\) to understand where \(f(x)\) is increasing or decreasing.

text:
Last time, we defined the derivative of a function \(f(x)\) at a single point \(x=a\). The value \(f'(a)\) measures the instantaneous rate of change of \(f(x)\) at \(x=a\), which we can see graphically as the slope of the line tangent to the graph of \(f(x)\) at that point.

title: Interpreting the Derivative
text:
When \(f(t)\) measures the position of an object in motion at time \(t\), the instantaneous rate of change \(f'(a)\) has a familiar meaning: it is the object’s instantaneous velocity at the moment \(t=a\). But derivatives show up in many contexts that have nothing to do with motion. What does the instantaneous rate of change mean when \(f(x)\) measures a population, a cost, the amount of rainfall, or the fuel efficiency of a car?
In general, the derivative of \(y=f(x)\) measures how sensitive the output \(y\) is to small, local changes in the input \(x\). If \(f'(a)\) is large in magnitude, then even a small change in \(x\) near \(x=a\) produces a large change in \(y\). If \(f'(a)\) is close to \(0\), then small changes in \(x\) near \(x=a\) barely affect \(y\) at all.
This gives us a practical way to interpret \(f'(a)\) in any context: we use it to estimate how much \(y\) changes when \(x\) changes by a small amount. Since \(f'(a)\) is the limit of average rates of change \(\frac{\Delta y}{\Delta x}\) over smaller and smaller intervals around \(x=a\), for a small change \(\Delta x\) we expect \[\frac{\Delta y}{\Delta x}\approx f'(a).\] Multiplying both sides by \(\Delta x\) gives us the key relationship for this section.






NotePractical Interpretation of \(f'(a)\)



If \(x\) changes from \(x=a\) to \(x=a+\Delta x\), where \(\Delta x\) is small, then the corresponding change in \(y=f(x)\) is approximately \[\Delta y \approx f'(a)\,\Delta x.\] In particular, the units of \(f'(a)\) are the units of \(y\) per unit of \(x\).


Keep in mind that this is a local estimate: it is only reliable when \(\Delta x\) is small, because the rate of change of \(f(x)\) may be quite different at points far away from \(x=a\).

During class this semester, we will spend most of our time working on and discussing problems. There will be assigned readings for each class that will help you prepare for these discussions.

title: Modeling with Families of Functions
text:
A mathematical model is an abstract mathematical representation of some object, idea, or relationship that exists in the real world. Creating a mathematical model usually involves making some simplifying assumptions about whatever it is we are trying to represent. Using data from measurements or other observations, we try to distill the essential properties that we want our model to capture. We use mathematical models to make estimate or predict, weigh and compare decisions, simulate experiments, and try to discover properties that may otherwise be difficult or costly to observe.
Be careful when drawing conclusions! Always consider the simplifying assumptions that were made when the model was created. Did we ignore anything that may impact our findings? Under what conditions is it reasonable to believe that the assumptions we made are realistic? These are all important things to include when communicating what you have learned in its real world context.

title: Modeling with Families of Functions
text:
What should you know?
The following families of functions are frequently used as the basis for mathematical models. How well do you know them? We will need to be able to:

Solve equations involving each of these types of functions.
Recognize properties of the function from its formula.

It is very helpful if you are familiar enough with each of these families of functions to be able to “see” what the graph looks like and sketch it out by hand without relying on a graphing tool.

Linear Functions
Our first question in creating a mathematical model for a relationship is often is it linear? Linear models are simple to understand and easy to work with. Our intuition often relies on linear thinking.
There are two common ways of writing a linear formula:
\[\begin{align}
&f(x)=mx+b & (\text{Slope-Intercept Form}) \\
&f(x)=m(x-x_0)+y_0 & (\text{Point-Slope Form})
\end{align}\]


Power Functions
Useful when modeling something that is strictly increasing or decreasing, but not in a linear way.
The formula is: \[f(x)=k x^p\] where the power, \(p\), can be any real number.


Absolute Value Function
Useful when you only need the magnitude of a value: \[ f(x)=|x|\]


Exponential Functions
We say a quantity is increasing or decreasing exponentially when it always changes by the same factor over each unit of time.
There are two different ways of writing exponential functions:
\[f(x)=ab^x = a(1+r)^x\]
where \(a\) is the initial value, \(b\) is the growth factor, and \(r\) is the growth rate,
\[f(x)=ae^{rx}\]
where again \(r\) is the continuous or relative growth rate and again \(a\) is the initial value.


Logarithmic Functions
Logarithms provide the inverse relationship for exponential growth. They are useful because they can convert something changing on an exponential scale to a linear scale.
The formula is: \[f(x)=\log_b(x)\] where \(b\) is the base of the logarithm.
Most often, we will use: \[\begin{align}
&f(x)=\log(x) & (\text{common log, } b=10)\\
&f(x)=\ln(x) & (\text{natural log, } b=e)
\end{align}\]


Trigonometric Functions
Frequently used when trying to model quantities that vary periodically. Also useful in problems involving geometry.
The three main trigonometric functions are:
\[f(x) = \sin(x),~ f(x) = \cos(x),~ f(x) = \tan(x)\]
Also useful are the corresponding reciprocal functions:
\[f(x) = \csc(x) = \frac{1}{\sin(x)},~ f(x) = \sec(x) = \frac{1}{\cos(x)},
f(x) = \cot(x) = \frac{1}{\tan(x)}\]
And inverse functions: \[f(x) = \arcsin(x) = \sin^{-1}(x),
~f(x) = \arccos(x) = \cos^{-1}(x),
~f(x) = \arctan(x) = \tan^{-1}(x)\]


Polynomial Functions
We use polynomials to model relationships that have one or more local extrema.
The two common ways of writing polynomials are:
\[\begin{align}
&f(x)=a_nx^n +a_{n-1}x^{n-1}+\ldots +a_1x + a_0 & (\text{Standard form}) \\[5pt]
&f(x)=a(x-z_1)^{m_1}(x-z_2)^{m_2}\cdot\ldots\cdot(x-z_k)^{m_k}
& (\text{Factored form})
\end{align}\]
In standard form, the \(a_k\)s are called coefficients; \(n\) is the degree of the polynomial and \(a_n\) is referred to as the leading coefficient.
In factored form, the \(z_k\)s are the zeros or roots of the polynomial and the \(m_k\)s are their multiplicities; \(a\) is the leading coefficient.


Rational Functions
Rational functions are useful when the relationship has asymptotic behavior. There are two kinds of asymptotes:

vertical asymptotes: the magnitude of the output value increases without bound near a particular input value
horizontal asymptotes: the output value of the function approaches a specific value as the input tends towards \(\pm\infty\).

Rational functions can be written as \[ f(x)=\frac{p(x)}{q(x)} \] where \(p(x)\) and \(q(x)\) are polynomials.

title: Limits & Continuity - Definitions and Intuition
text:
When computing a limit, we are trying to determine the end result of an indefinite process. Like with the light switch example in the Unit 1 Overview, some indefinite processes do not yield a final outcome. In these cases, we say that the limit of the process does not exist.
In other instances, like with the value of \(0.999\ldots\), we will be able to see that the outcomes of the process (\(0.9\), \(0.99\), \(0.999\), \(\ldots\)) become infinitesimally close to a specific value and we define this value to be the limit of the process.
The process we are interested in here is the value a function \(f(x)\) approaches as \(x\) approaches a particular input value \(x=a\) or as \(x\) tends towards \(\infty\) or \(-\infty\). We use the following notation when trying to compute the limit in this context: \[\lim_{x\to a}f(x).\]
Note that \(\displaystyle\lim_{x\to a}f(x)\) and \(f(a)\) are asking two different questions:

\(\displaystyle\lim_{x\to a}f(x)\) is asking us to examine the behavior of the output values of \(f\) as the input values get closer and closer to \(x=a\); at no point in this process do we plug in \(x=a\).
\(f(a)\) is asking for the output value that we get when we plug in \(x=a\).

In some cases, these questions have the same answer. We say that the function is continuous at \(x=a\) when this happens. In other cases, they do not. But it is always important to keep in mind that these are two distinct questions!
Here are some formal definitions for the different kinds of limits we will use in this context:

Definition 1 (Limit) For a given real number \(a\), we write that \[\lim_{x\to a}f(x)=L\] when there is a real number \(L\) such that the values of \(f(x)\) can be made arbitrarily close to \(L\) by plugging in any \(x\) value that is sufficiently close to, but not equal to \(a\). In this case, we say that the limit of \(f(x)\) as \(x\) approaches \(a\) exists and equals \(L\).


Definition 2 (Limits at Infinity) We write that \[\lim_{x\to \infty}f(x)=L\] when there is a real number \(L\) such that the values of \(f(x)\) can be made arbitrarily close to \(L\) by plugging in sufficiently large values for \(x\).
We write \[\lim_{x\to -\infty}f(x)=L\] when there is a real number \(L\) such that the values of \(f(x)\) can be made arbitrarily close to \(L\) by plugging in negative values for \(x\) that are sufficiently large in magnitude.
In these cases, we say that the limit of \(f(x)\) as \(x\) approaches infinity or negative infinity exists and equals \(L\).


Definition 3 For a given real number \(a\), we write that \[\lim_{x\to a^+}f(x)=L\] if there is a real number \(L\) such that the values of \(f(x)\) can be made arbitrarily close to \(L\) by plugging in any \(x\) value that sufficiently close to, but greater than \(a\).
We write that \[\lim_{x\to a^-}f(x)=L\] if there is a real number \(L\) such that the values of \(f(x)\) can be made arbitrarily close to \(L\) by plugging in any \(x\) value that sufficiently close to, but less than \(a\).
In these cases, we say that the limit of \(f(x)\) as \(x\) approaches a from the right (\(x\to a^+\)), or from the left (\(x\to a^-\)), exists and equals \(L\).

Definition of Continuity
One property we frequently look for in functions is their continuity. This is a particular nice property to have if \(y=f(x)\) is the model for some real world relationship. If \(f\) is continuous at \(x=a\) and \(f(a)=b\), then we know that sufficiently small errors in our input value (e.g. maybe \(a\) gets rounded to the nearest 0.01) will produce an output value that is within some desired margin of error around \(b\).
In terms of limits, as noted above, knowing a function is continuous at \(x=a\) makes evaluating the limit really easy—all we have to do in this case is plug in \(x=a\).
Here is our formal definition:

Definition 4 (Continuity) We say that \(f(x)\) is continuous at \(x=a\) if \[\lim_{x\to a}f(x)=f(a)\]

title: Evaluating Limits Using Algebra
text:
Graphs and data tables are helpful for developing our intuition about limits. They can be used as the basis for making a reasonable guess as to whether \(\displaystyle\lim_{x\to a}f(x)\) exists and estimating its value if it does. However, these approaches fall short of providing conclusive proof.
When using a computational tool to create a data table or graph, we are limited by its level of precision (it can only compute a certain number of decimal places) and its finite-ness. Making a conclusion about some indefinite process based on a finite number of measurements can be treacherous, even when done carefully!
Today, we will go over some analytical and algebraic approaches that are more robust and can be used in certain cases to show why a limit does or does not exist and determine its value.
Before we proceed: Remember that if we know the function is continuous at \(x=a\), all we have to do is plug in to evaluate \(\displaystyle\lim_{x\to a}f(x)\)! This works, for example, if \(f(x)\) can be written as the combination of elementary functions and \(x=a\) is in its domain1
The algebraic techniques discussed here are for analyzing what happens when \(a\) is not in the domain of \(f(x)\), particularly when we arrive at indeterminate forms when trying to use limit properties.

Last time, we defined the derivative of a function \(f(x)\) at a single point \(x=a\). The value \(f'(a)\) measures the instantaneous rate of change of \(f(x)\) at \(x=a\), which we can see graphically as the slope of the line tangent to the graph of \(f(x)\) at that point.

title: The Second Derivative
text:
We already have a good understanding of functions with constant slope. These are linear functions. If the slope is positive, the function is increasing; if the slope is negative, the function is decreasing.
Over the past few sections, we developed a way to measure the slope of a function when the slope is not constant. The derivative \(f'(x)\) tells us the slope of \(f(x)\) at each point. When the slope of a function is always changing, the graph is no longer a straight line, it will bend and curve.
In this section, we discuss \(f''(x)\), the second derivative of \(f(x)\). Since \(f'(x)\) is itself a function, we can take its derivative to find the rate of change of the slope of \(f(x)\).

Definition 1 (The Second Derivative) The second derivative of \(f(x)\), written \(f''(x)\), is the derivative of \(f'(x)\). The value \(f''(a)\) measures the instantaneous rate of change of the slope of \(f(x)\) at \(x=a\).

While the values of \(f'(x)\) tell us where \(f(x)\) is increasing, decreasing or constant, the values of \(f''(x)\) will tell us where \(f'(x)\) is increasing, decreasing or constant. This will allow us to use \(f''(x)\) to determine how \(f(x)\) is curved. We call this property the concavity of \(f(x)\).
